title: Cricket Frenzy Grips Indian and Pakistani Expatriates Across the Gulf
excerpt: From Friday-morning games on Riyadh's open grounds to crowded restaurants during India-Pakistan clashes, cricket remains the cultural lifeline of South Asian expatriates — and Saudi Arabia is building a sporting future around it.
body:
• Arab News reporting from Riyadh captures undimmed cricket passion among Indian and Pakistani expatriates, who track matches on phones at work and gather for watch parties after hours.
  • Friday games on open grounds in neighborhoods like Hai Al-Naseem and Diriyah are a weekly ritual, and India-Pakistan clashes remain the ultimate draw.
  • Saudi Arabia has institutionalized the passion: the Saudi Arabian Cricket Federation, a National Cricket Championship, and Vision 2030 backing for a competitive national side.
  • For millions of South Asian workers in the Kingdom, the game is a connection to home — and a rare bridge across communities.

At a Pakistani restaurant in Riyadh, the tables were pushed aside and every eye was on the screen. Arab News reporters found Indian and Pakistani expatriates watching a PSL game together — partisans of rival franchises, united by the one thing that reliably empties the Kingdom's South Asian neighborhoods on match nights: cricket.

"Cricket matches have created a frenzy among the expatriates and their families," Faiz Al-Najdi, who has lived in Riyadh for decades, told Arab News. "Especially the matches played between archrivals India and Pakistan — a treat to watch."

The game the expats built

Long before cricket had federations or championships in Saudi Arabia, it had the expats. Millions of workers from cricket-mad South Asia — India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Afghanistan — built the game from scratch: Friday matches on stone-strewn lots beside shopping malls, tape-ball tournaments in parking lots, leagues run on WhatsApp groups and scoresheets balanced on pickup trucks.

An AFP dispatch from Riyadh once captured the scene outside Granada Mall, where Indian players made do with a rock-strewn sand pitch beside a multi-lane road. "You don't find anything like entertainment in the ultra-conservative Islamic kingdom," one player said at the time. For drivers, shopkeepers and engineers working long weeks far from home, Friday cricket was — and remains — the release valve.

"Cricket is a game that has an almost magical ability. I just love playing cricket."

— Mohammed Serajuddin, Indian expatriate in Riyadh, to Arab News

Serajuddin described the weekly ritual: "Every Friday and whenever there is time to play, mostly on public holidays, we gather at some grounds, open spaces to play cricket, mostly in Hai Al-Naseem district or in the Diriyah area."

The rivalry that stops everything

Nothing moves the needle like India versus Pakistan. The two nations have not played a bilateral series in more than a decade and meet only in global or regional tournaments, which makes every encounter appointment viewing — and in the Gulf, where both diasporas live side by side, the build-up spills into restaurants, majlis gatherings and office debates.

The emotions are complicated. Ahead of a recent high-voltage clash, Mumbai graphic designer Vidya Mansinghani told reporters she would watch from home rather than host a party, torn between patriotism and the pull of the game. "I am a patriot, and what happened in Pahalgam was extremely painful," she said. "But at the same time, cricket is part of our culture." Others see the fixture as a bridge: Harris Arshad, a project manager from Islamabad, argued the match "should proceed despite tensions, as sports can bridge divides and promote goodwill."

Back in Riyadh, the workday constrains the ritual. "Expatriates in Saudi Arabia are constrained to just follow the scores of these matches via their smartphones," Al-Najdi said. "As the ODI and T20 matches are split between day and night, we enjoy watching these matches after office hours in our homes — with the families or with a group of friends."

What it means for the diaspora

For Indians in the Gulf — millions of whom live and work across the Kingdom and the Emirates — cricket is identity infrastructure. It is how a new arrival in Dammam or Jeddah finds friends within a week, how children born abroad learn where their parents come from, and how India and Pakistan, so often at odds on the map, share tables, screens and jokes on Friday nights. The frenzy Arab News documented is not really about any single tournament. It is about belonging, staged one match at a time.

The Kingdom's cricket ambitions

Saudi Arabia has noticed — and is investing. The Saudi Arabian Cricket Federation was established in 2020 under Prince Saud bin Mishal Al-Saud, and its National Cricket Championship is now the largest tournament in the Kingdom's history. Under the Vision 2030 sports push, cricket sits alongside football, Formula 1 and boxing as a priority: the Kingdom is directing serious resources at facilities, coaching and a competitive national team, which has already secured back-to-back ACC Men's Challenger Cup victories.

If the trajectory holds, the next generation of expat kids playing on Riyadh's open grounds may grow up with something their parents never had: a Saudi national cricket team worth cheering — built, in no small part, by the frenzy they inherited.
image_caption: Sharjah Cricket Stadium, a popular venue for matches drawing large South Asian expatriate crowds in the Gulf. Cricket frenzy is gripping Indian and Pakistani expatriates across the Gulf.
nri_angle: For millions of Indian and Pakistani workers in the Gulf, cricket is home in portable form — and Saudi Arabia's cricket push could soon give their children a national team of their own.
author: Diaspora Desk
